candidates.context: In the centre of the MWC a high grade Rare Earths Oxide (REO) deposit known as the Central Lanthanide Deposit (CLD) has been defined in the goethite rich saprolite, iron-silica nodules and the apatite rich layers of the regolith. The rare earth oxides are found predominantly in monazite with minor cerianite, florencite and xenotime. The high grades are believed to be caused by the bulk of the REO’s remaining in the regolith over the central portion of the MWC whilst the more mobile carbonate minerals were removed by fluids during the weathering process.

3. GEOLOGY & MINERALISATION

3.1    Regional Geology

The mining tenements cover a near  vertical carbonatite plug known as the Mt Weld
Carbonatite (MWC). The MWC has intruded strongly deformed Archean volcanic and
sedimentary rocks of the Laverton Tectonic Zone (LTZ) (Gower, 1976; Hallberg 1985). The
exploration tenements cover the LTZ formation to the west of the MWC and the rocks are
predominantly felsic and mafic volcanic rocks. To the east of the MWC are predominantly
mafic and sedimentary rocks. A series of Proterozoic dolerite dykes have intruded the LTZ in
the project area with one of these linear dykes also intruding the MWC from the north-west to
the south-east.

Subsequent to the dolerite intrusions, there has been a long period of erosion lowering the
surface by over 2 kilometres over the MWC and LTZ formations with an extensive drainage
system developed over the area by the Late Eocene. Since the Late Eocene the on-set of
dry conditions has resulted in these drainage systems to be filled with clay. One of these clay
filled drainage systems covers a portion of the MWC.

From the quaternary to present day the MWC, the lake sediments, and the surrounding LTZ
have been covered by a layer of alluvial gravels and sands washed in by sheet wash from
the hills 10 kilometres to the east. This layer of alluvium is approximately 25 metres thick in
the project area.

3.2    Local Geology

The MWC is a sub-vertical pipe like intrusion approximately 3.5 kilometres in diameter. The
primary carbonatite rock is medium grain sovite (calcitic carbonatite) with lesser beforsite
(dolomitic carbonatite) with minor zones of silico-carbonatite. Locally apatite and magnetite
may dominate the carbonatite phase. Within the MWC is approximately 20-30% xenolithic
material particularly around the margins where it comes in contact with the LTZ rocks. The
xenolithc material varies from being almost totally digested flow bands through to hard edged
metasomatised boulders. Most of the xenolithic material has a mafic origin.

The MWC has had the development of a complex regolith over  it between the end of the
Permian glacial period and the Late Eocene. The regolith contains a number of minerals of
economic importance with possible exploitation of the Rare Earth Oxides (Lanthanides and
Yttrium), Rare Metals (Niobium, Tantalum and Titanium) and Phosphate. See figure 3 for
local geology and the deposits that have been defined by previous drilling. The regolith is
layered with an apatite-manganese rich zone at the bottom, a goethite rich saprolite above
the apatite- manganese zone that grades up into an iron-silica rich nodule zone and then the
surface is a silica-iron rich cap-rock. See Figures 4 for a diagrammatic cross-section of the
local geology.

Cutting into the carbonatite regolith are areas of clays that in-filled the drainage systems. The
clays are plastic smectite clays (montmorillite) derived from the surrounding LTZ rocks. In
some areas the clays have been replaced with calcrete by percolating calcite fluids.  It is
probable that the calcite in the fluids is derived from the carbonatite. In the upper part of the
clays iron leaching from the alluvium above has created large nodules of haematite in the
upper 5 metres of the clays. In some areas dense zones of iron pisolites have collected on
the surface of the clays and were the final stage of deposition in the drainage system.

The final geological unit deposited in the tenement area is the alluvium washed in from the
hills in the east. The alluvium is 20- 25 metres thick and consists of iron and quartz rich sand
and gravel. The alluvium has been laterised during its deposition with the surface being quite
hard.

3.3    Mineralisation

The carbonatite regolith is a source of a number of different zones of mineralisation.  In the
centre of the MWC a high grade Rare Earths Oxide (REO) deposit known as the Central
Lanthanide Deposit (CLD) has been defined in the goethite rich saprolite, iron-silica nodules
and the apatite rich layers of the regolith. The rare earth oxides are found predominantly in
monazite with minor cerianite, florencite and xenotime. The high grades are believed to be
caused by the bulk of the REO’s remaining in the regolith over the central portion of the
MWC  whilst the more mobile carbonate minerals were removed by  fluids during the
weathering process. The bulk of the REO’s are the light REO’s but on the eastern side of the
CLD there is a higher concentration of xenotime and florencite. Hence a higher concentration
of heavy REO are present in this area. At present the first campaign of mining has occurred
on the high grade light REO’s and the ore has been stockpiled for processing in a floatation
plant which began operations in May 2011. The heavy REO zone was defined by drilling in
2009 and has been called the Duncan Deposit to distinguish it from the light REO material.
The entire carbonatite regolith contains some REO’s usually between 0.5 and 4% REO.

In the north-eastern and south-western portions of the carbonatite regolith are rare metals
deposits known as Anchor, Crown and Coors containing niobium, tantalum and titanium. The
rare metals are contained within the same layers of the regolith as the REO’s in the CLD.
The element with the highest economic significance within the rare metals is the niobium but
the others combined with the niobium has in the past been investigated in metallurgical
studies to see if all the minerals can be exploited economically.

The other zone of mineralisation that could possibly be exploited economically  is the
phosphate in the apatite. The phosphate is in high concentrations in the apatite rich layer
throughout the entire carbonatite regolith. Previous owners of the tenements carried out a
feasibility study on mining and processing the phosphate to make fertiliser from the Swan
and Emu Deposits in the northern portion of the carbonatite regolith.

       Modelling

   4.3.1   Introduction

The previous resource model was developed in 2011-2012 using  all the drill-hole data
available for the Central Lanthanide Deposit (CLD) and Duncan Deposit (DD). The model
was developed after a large close spaced drilling program on the western side of the CLD
was carried out in 2011 completing the delineation of the CLD to indicated status.

Lynas was required to go through a number of due diligences which involved reviewing the
previous 2011-2012 REO mineral resources and ore reserves. One of the reviewers carried
out a very detailed review of the mineral resources and ore reserves. The detailed review
found some mistakes and issues with the model. Overall the review found the ore reserves
were reasonable but the model could be improved.

   4.3.2   Updated Resource Modelling 2014

Before the external review an internal review of the model found other areas to the external
review that could be improved and enhanced. It was decided to redo the model in late 2014
to improve the model from the one used for the ore reserves in 2012. It was also decided to
relax the parameters used to define the inferred resources so that the mineralisation in the

7. WATER MANAGEMENT

Lynas has been investigating tailings dewatering and water recycling options for a number of
years (Tailing Management and Water Treatment System). Decant water is recovered from
the tailings storage facility (TSF) and recycled to or reused in flotation plant. The originally
installed plant failed to meet the design objectives, leading to an accumulation of water in the
tailings storage facility, which hampered the drying of the tailings. The tailings need to dried
to 30% moisture to maximise storage in the TSF and meet closure requirements.

There are/were three components to the project:

        a.     Evaluation of tailings dewatering options.

        b.     Decant water clarification and filtration.

        c.     Upgrades to the existing RO plant to allow processing the clarified and/or
                 filtered water.

A pilot plant trial of a dewatering option using a screw press was completed in April & May
2015 (See Appendix D for report). Although the screw press  trial was successful, the
operation has decided  to  continue  to use Enhanced  Tailings Dewatering (ETD)  for
dewatering.

A number of  clarification,  filtration and RO investigations have been completed  in the
reporting  period  including Membrane  Futures  tests  of membrane  fibres  to  increase
permeability and lower TMP increase rates and Ishigaki polishing filter trials. The operation
has a working flow sheet to recycle water from the TSF, but further work is required to
optimise the cleaning regimes for the ultrafiltration and RO stages and expand the capacity
of the water retirement plant.

8. MINING AND PROCESSING

During the reporting period no mining has been carried out. The only activity within the Mt
Weld open pit involved a rip test in October 2015 on the current pit floor using a D10 dozer.

The flotation concentrator for extracting a rare earth concentrate continued operations at Mt
Weld on a campaign basis to match the Malaysian cracking production. For the reporting
period the flotation plant had milled 111,227 tonnes of ore to produce 36,784 tonnes of
concentrate containing 14,213 tonnes of REO.

A number of issues have been identified with the water balance for the concentrator and tails
storage facilities (TSF) resulting in the TSF filling up a lot quicker than expected. To alleviate
these issues a considerable amount of work has been carried out on designing a system to
de-water the tails and increase the size of the TSF. During the reporting period a second
TSF has been constructed to increase the tails holding capacity.
